headline: Trader charged 14 times for same misclick now receiving loyalty points from SEBI
body:
Q: Ramesh, you were recently fined fourteen times by fourteen different regulatory bodies for accidentally typing an extra zero into a trade. How are you processing this?

A: It was a chaotic Tuesday. I kept getting alerts on my phone, my watch, and even my smart fridge. But then, the regulator announced this new framework to scrap duplicate fines, and suddenly, my status changed from 'Debtor' to 'Gold-Tier Regulatory Participant'.

Q: Are you saying your fines were converted into a rewards program?

A: Precisely. Because I triggered the same violation across multiple exchanges simultaneously, the new system decided I wasn’t a repeat offender, but a 'High-Frequency Regulatory Engager'. They sent me a digital voucher for 4,000 points which I can redeem for either a branded keychain or a 'Get Out Of Jail' card for my next accidental decimal point error.

Q: Do you feel the system has finally achieved balance?

A: Absolutely. I used to be stressed, but now I look forward to clicking the wrong button. If I make the same mistake on three more platforms today, I qualify for the 'Diamond Platinum Compliance' lounge access at the stock exchange café.
caption: Trading errors are finally being recognized for the high-frequency events they are. Who knew fiscal discipline came with lounge access? #StockMarket #FinanceHumor #SEBI #TradingLife (satire)
igHook: Would you purposely trigger a fine if it meant getting free coffee at the exchange?

sourceHeadline.title: SEBI proposing framework to scrap duplicate fines across exchanges for same violation

judgeVerdict.reasoning: Candidate 6 provides a unique spin on the 'duplicate fine' trope by introducing a 'loyalty rewards' bureaucratic absurdity. It avoids the nihilism of the other entries by focusing on the trader finding a silver lining in a broken system, maintaining a tone of warm, absurd resignation rather than just complaining about fees.

safetyVerdict.reasoning: The article uses a fictionalized scenario to satirize bureaucratic processes and regulatory bodies. The character 'Ramesh' is a generic archetype, and the piece makes no defamatory claims about real individuals or specific professional misconduct.
